section: 1 Introduction
text: Watermarking and fingerprinting constitute the foundational technical infrastructure for securing large language models (LLMs) across their full lifecycle—from pretraining data provenance and fine-tuning lineage to API-mediated deployment and edge-device adaptation—yet they remain conceptually and operationally distinct from broader AI safety, privacy, and robustness paradigms.

section: 1 Introduction
text: Unlike safety guardrails that constrain harmful outputs or privacy-preserving mechanisms that mitigate membership inference or data leakage, watermarking and fingerprinting are *provenance-first* primitives: they encode verifiable claims of origin, ownership, or usage into either model behavior or its artifacts, enabling forensic accountability without altering functional intent.

section: 2.2 Detection Modality Spectrum: From White-Box Verification to Black-Box Auditing

section: 2.2 Detection Modality Spectrum: From White-Box Verification to Black-Box Auditing
text: We formalize this as a three-tiered continuum: white-box (full parameter access), gray-box (intermediate representations—logits, attention maps, or architectural priors), and black-box (query-response behavior only)—each imposing distinct constraints on adversary capability, verification latency, forensic rigor, and real-world deployability.

section: 2.3 Formal Security Properties: A Unified Information-Theoretic and Cryptographic Framework
text: This subsection establishes a unifying formal framework that transcends heuristic claims of “robustness” or “stealth” by axiomatizing four interdependent security properties—detectability, robustness, unforgeability, and collusion resistance—through the complementary lenses of information theory, cryptography, and game-theoretic adversarial modeling.

section: 2.3 Formal Security Properties: A Unified Information-Theoretic and Cryptographic Framework
text: Crucially, these properties are not independent; their simultaneous satisfaction is constrained by fundamental limits exposed in seminal impossibility results, which prove that no watermark can be both *strongly robust* (i.e., resistant to quality-preserving perturbations) and *computationally undetectable* without degrading output fidelity—a consequence of the attacker’s access to a quality oracle and a perturbation oracle inducing an efficiently mixing walk over high-quality outputs.

section: 2.3 Formal Security Properties: A Unified Information-Theoretic and Cryptographic Framework
